case_study_insert.main_stem: SwiftShine Cleaning (SSC) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2017 by Noah Swift, it provides eco-friendly domestic and office cleaning and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. SSC plans to invest $560,000 in a low-moisture carpet-cleaning plant and electric van fleet, financed by a $320,000 five-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year, each a cleaning job. Household demand has grown as more families outsource cleaning. SSC faces two problems: staff absenteeism has reached 11% and complaints about missed appointments are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report, Q4 2025: The eco-cleaning pilot completed 24,000 jobs last quarter with a re-clean rate of 2.9%, down from 4.7% a year ago. Customer complaints about missed appointments fell from 73 to 31 per month. Average job completion time is 96 minutes. A survey of 550 household customers found 74% would pay up to $0.70 more for eco-friendly cleaning and 61% check environmental credentials before booking. Records show 26 of 80 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new low-moisture machines; external courses cost $560 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of SwiftShine Cleaning for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 8.3% from $13.25 to $14.35 per hour, strongly affecting labour-intensive services. (3) Eco-cleaning product and vehicle-energy input costs have risen 12.7% year-on-year, cleaning-services inflation is 7.4%, and household spending on paid cleaning grew 4.6% over the same period.

questions.question_text: SSC plans to fund part of its $560,000 carpet-cleaning plant with a $320,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SSC of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or compulsory repayments, so the $240,000 from past profits protects cash flow while SSC meets fixed costs of $264,000 a year. Cash kept can absorb the 12.7% rise in eco-product and vehicle-energy costs without raising the $12.00 price, preserving the $6.00 contribution on 100,000 jobs.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids pledging security for the $320,000 loan, so the new plant and van fleet cannot be repossessed if demand slows. It leaves Noah Swift's ownership intact, since no lender can impose conditions. Internal funds are available at once, letting SSC replace the machines behind the 2.9% re-clean rate and reduce the 11% absenteeism disrupting appointments. Fixed costs of $264,000 a year are a real burden for a company founded only in 2017, so avoiding interest on the $320,000 loan protects its early growth; the electric vans also need capital, and preserving cash protects the 100,000-job target.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to SSC, its plant, costs and services.

questions.question_text: SSC is promoting its new eco-friendly cleaning service. Consider advertising in local newspapers, sponsoring a community sports team, or targeted social media and email marketing to households. Which should SSC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertising: Newspaper adverts would reach households in SSC's service area and build local awareness, but print readership is falling and the static message cannot show the eco-friendly difference. For an 80-staff company committing $560,000 to a new plant, wide untargeted circulation wastes spend and gives little measurable response.

Community sports team sponsorship: Sponsoring a local team would build goodwill and brand visibility in the community, which suits a household service, and could support the 61% of surveyed customers who check environmental credentials. However, it is a costly one-off with no direct booking mechanism; with 550 customers surveyed and 24,000 jobs last quarter, a kit deal alone cannot drive 100,000 jobs a year.

Targeted social media and email marketing: Digital marketing to households can show before-and-after eco-cleaning results to the 74% who would pay $0.70 more, highlight environmental credentials, and track bookings cheaply. Content can be refreshed as the 2.9% re-clean rate falls. The weakness is that households may ignore adverts and trust comes from reviews, so SSC should pair messages with customer testimonials. With fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a measurable low-cost channel is preferable to untargeted print.

Recommendation: SSC should choose targeted social media and email marketing, with a small local sponsorship for goodwill. It reaches the 74% willing to pay $0.70 more cheaply and can run continuously for 100,000 jobs, unlike a one-off kit deal. Newspapers are rejected as declining and untargeted; major team sponsorship is rejected as costly and unable to deliver measurable bookings for a business servicing a $320,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to SSC's survey or service.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SSC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options with a justified recommendation that explains why newspapers and major sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: SSC has hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and absenteeism has reached 11%. Explain two benefits for SSC of introducing team working among its cleaning staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets the 80 staff cover for absent colleagues and share routes, reducing disruption from the 11% absenteeism rate and the missed appointments that generated 73 complaints a month. Teams can also pool ideas on the new low-moisture machines, helping push the 2.9% re-clean rate lower and protecting the 24,000 jobs completed last quarter.

Point 2: Working in teams satisfies social needs in Maslow's hierarchy and raises job satisfaction, which should improve attendance and reduce complaints. Democratic leadership supports this approach, and teams can learn from the 26 of 80 staff already trained, easing the $560 per employee external-course cost while the $560,000 plant beds in. Teams let cleaners share the new low-moisture machines and the skills of the 26 of 80 staff already trained. In a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership, team briefings also give staff a voice about the missed appointments behind 73 complaints a month.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of team working (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SSC's absenteeism, complaints, training and structure.

questions.question_text: SSC must train 26 of its 80 staff on the new low-moisture machines. Consider on-the-job training or external courses costing $560 per employee. Which should SSC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the job site is specific to SSC's own low-moisture machines and eco-products, costs no fees, and keeps the 26 staff earning while they learn. That protects the 24,000 jobs completed last quarter and the fall in re-clean rate from 4.7% to 2.9%. Drawbacks are that trainer-cleaners finish fewer jobs, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate to support the 61% of customers who check environmental credentials.

External courses: At $560 per employee, training all 26 costs $14,560 ($560 x 26), affordable against the $560,000 investment and providing structured, recognised skills. However, it removes 26 of 80 staff from rounds temporarily, worsening the 11% absenteeism and missed appointments, and generic content may not match SSC's exact machines, so follow-up coaching would still be needed. The $14,560 competes with the $264,000 fixed costs and the $320,000 loan. Since 61% of customers check environmental credentials, some formal proof of competence is valuable, but it can be phased in rather than bought for all 26 staff at once.

Decision: SSC should choose on-the-job training initially, adding short external courses for senior cleaners later. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing job capacity while absenteeism is 11%; full external training is rejected because the $14,560 and the loss of 26 staff would disrupt the 100,000-job plan and appointment reliability, and certificates can be added once the plant is running smoothly, with on-site coaching correcting re-clean faults immediately, senior cleaners mentoring the rest so rounds stay fully staffed; a short external course for senior cleaners would still answer the 61% credentials check.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to SSC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the benefits and drawbacks of each method in the context of SSC's costs, capacity and staffing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and refers to cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SSC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $264,000 ÷ ($12.00 − $6.00) = $264,000 ÷ $6.00 = 44,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 44,000 cleaning jobs a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.00 − $6.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SSC's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 44,000-job break-even output with 100,000 actual jobs to find a margin of safety of 56,000 jobs (100,000 − 44,000), showing the $560,000 plant can absorb a demand fall.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution to assess the survey: at 100,000 jobs a $0.70 premium would add $70,000 (100,000 x $0.70), funding the $560 training courses.
3. Check that contribution covers fixed costs of $264,000 and interest on the $320,000 loan before adding vans, so finance costs do not raise break-even.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $8.64 ($264,000 ÷ 100,000 + $6.00) each quarter to detect waste from the 2.9% re-clean rate and judge whether 12.7% input-cost inflation is absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 44,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: a margin of safety of 56,000 jobs against 100,000 output; a $0.70 premium adding $70,000; covering $264,000 fixed costs and $320,000 loan interest; and unit-cost benchmarking at $8.64 to track 12.7% input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SSC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has SSC's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 14.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 21.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.1%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $840,000 on revenue of $2,100,000 in 2024 gives 840 ÷ 2,100 = 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $1,125,000 on $2,500,000 gives 1,125 ÷ 2,500 = 45.0%. Operating profit of $294,000 ÷ $2,100,000 = 14.0% in 2024 and $375,000 ÷ $2,500,000 = 15.0% in 2025. The return on capital employed divides operating profit by capital employed: $294,000 ÷ $1,400,000 = 21.0% and $375,000 ÷ $1,700,000 = 22.1%. Cost of sales of $1,260,000 and $1,375,000 reconciles exactly with gross profit in both years.

Evaluation: Every measure improved. The rise from 40.0% to 45.0% shows more revenue retained after direct costs, as revenue grew $400,000 while cost of sales rose only $115,000, so most of the growth was retained as gross profit, while interest payable fell by $6,000. Operating profitability increased from 14.0% to 15.0%, indicating overheads were controlled as jobs grew. The return on capital improved from 21.0% to 22.1%, so the $1,700,000 of capital employed is working harder, which supports the $560,000 plant. Interest payable fell from $36,000 to $30,000, easing the burden on profit.

Conclusion: SSC's financial performance has improved. All three margins rose, the return on capital strengthened and interest payable fell, leaving the company better able to service the $320,000 loan. Management should still reduce the 11% absenteeism and missed appointments, which could erode these gains.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SSC of offering eco-friendly cleaning.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-friendly cleaning matches the survey finding that 74% of customers would pay up to $0.70 more and 61% check environmental credentials. At 100,000 jobs a $0.70 premium could add $70,000 (100,000 x $0.70), protecting the $6.00 contribution per job against 12.7% input-cost inflation and supporting the $560,000 plant. The eco positioning also appeals to the 61% who check credentials, helping retain the household demand that has grown since 2017.

Disadvantage: Eco-friendly products and the electric van fleet raise the $6.00 variable cost per job and the $264,000 fixed costs, squeezing margins unless the $0.70 premium is widely accepted. With 11% absenteeism and 26 of 80 staff untrained, any failure to use the low-moisture machines correctly would lift the 2.9% re-clean rate and worsen the missed-appointment complaints. Since the insert gives no split of the $6.00 variable cost, the exact margin effect cannot be quantified and remains a qualitative risk.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SSC's survey data, costs and plant.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 8.3% minimum wage increase and the 12.7% rise in input costs will affect SSC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If SSC's $320,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% x $320,000 = $2,400 a year (0.0075 x $320,000), modest beside fixed costs of $264,000, and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates may also reduce household spending on paid cleaning, but SSC can mostly remove the direct risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (8.3%, to $14.35 an hour): With a workforce of 80 and output of 100,000 jobs, labour productivity is 100,000 ÷ 80 = 1,250 jobs per worker. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented; the defensible check is whether each worker maintains about 1,250 jobs. With absenteeism at 11%, a productivity fall would raise unit labour costs and shrink the $6.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (12.7% in eco-products and energy): The insert states a $6.00 variable cost per job but does not decompose it, so only an illustrative upper bound is proper. If the whole $6.00 rose 12.7%, that is 12.7% x $6.00 = $0.762, about $0.76 per job; across 100,000 jobs that is roughly $76,200 a year (100,000 x $0.76). Even a smaller $0.55 rise would cost $55,000 a year (100,000 x $0.55), pulling contribution from $6.00 toward about $5.45.

Conclusion: The 12.7% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It touches all 100,000 jobs and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution supporting the $560,000 plant, and at up to about $76,200 a year it is far bigger than the conditional $2,400 interest cost. The wage rise is serious but cannot be quantified from the insert and depends on 1,250-job productivity holding, while interest risk is small and fixable. SSC should negotiate supplier deals and recover part of the increase through the $0.70 eco premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to SSC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SSC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller, with arithmetic shown from insert figures.
